title: Queues vs logs
scopeHtml:
Scope: SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka, when each fits, consumer groups and ordering.

Scope: SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka, when each fits, consumer groups and ordering.

notes.title: Why queues exist
notes.html:
A queue lets a producer hand off work and move on, while a consumer processes it later at its own pace. It decouples two things in time (the consumer can be down or slow), in speed (absorbs bursts) and in scale (add consumers independently).

Worked example. A sale causes 5,000 orders/s for 60 s, while the email service handles 500/s. Without a queue, 4,500 requests/s fail or time out. With a queue the backlog grows by 4,500/s x 60 s = 270,000 messages (at 1 KB, 270 MB) and drains in about 540 s once traffic falls. The user got an instant "order placed".

Industry examples. Uber, Swiggy and Zomato use queues/streams between order, dispatch and notification services. Amazon SQS processes enormous volumes of work items; Shopify uses Kafka widely.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen order rail: waiters pin tickets and move on; the chef cooks as fast as possible.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a queue for a flow the user needs an immediate result from (needs sync response, or a status poll).
  • Not saying what happens when the queue is full or the consumer is down.

notes.title: Queue vs log: the core difference
notes.html:
A traditional queue deletes a message once it is consumed. A log keeps messages for a set time and consumers just track a position (offset).

  • Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ): message goes to one consumer, is acknowledged, then removed. Good for "do this job once". Replaying means re-publishing.
  • Log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar): an append-only ordered file. Many independent consumers read the same data at their own offsets. Replay is just resetting the offset.

Decision gravity. A queue is simpler for task distribution. A log is best when several systems want the same events (search indexing, analytics, cache invalidation) or you need replay after a bug. Moving a system from queue to log later is painful because consumers' ack semantics differ: nearly a one-way door.

Industry examples. LinkedIn built Kafka because many systems needed the same activity stream. Banks use RabbitMQ/IBM MQ for transactional work items.

Everyday analogy. A queue is a pile of letters that you throw away after reading. A log is a diary on a shelf that anyone can read from any page.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling Kafka "just a faster queue". Retention and replay change how you design.
  • Forgetting that with a log, a slow consumer does not delete anything; it just lags.

notes.title: SQS and RabbitMQ in practice
notes.html:
SQS is a managed, almost infinitely scalable queue; RabbitMQ is a feature-rich broker you run (or rent).

SQS:

  • Standard queue: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering (duplicates and reordering happen).
  • FIFO queue: strict order per MessageGroupId, exactly-once processing within a 5-minute dedup window using MessageDeduplicationId; throughput limited (about 300 msg/s per API action without batching, 3,000 with batching; higher with high-throughput mode; confirm current quotas).
  • Visibility timeout (default 30 s): after a consumer receives a message it is hidden; if not deleted in time, it reappears and is processed again. Max message size 256 KB (check docs). Dead-letter queue via a maxReceiveCount redrive policy.

RabbitMQ: producers publish to an exchange (direct, topic, fanout, headers) which routes by binding to queues. Consumers ack manually; unacked messages are redelivered. Features: priorities, TTLs, delayed messages (plugin), per-message routing, quorum queues for replication. Throughput is tens of thousands msg/s per node, below Kafka for bulk streaming.

{ "RedrivePolicy": { "deadLetterTargetArn": "arn:aws:sqs:...:orders-dlq", "maxReceiveCount": 5 },
  "VisibilityTimeout": 60 }

Worked example. A video-transcoding job takes up to 4 minutes. If the SQS visibility timeout is 30 s, the message reappears while worker 1 is still busy and worker 2 starts the same job. Fix: set the timeout above the max job time (say 300 s) or extend it with a heartbeat.

Industry examples. Many AWS-based systems use SQS plus Lambda; RabbitMQ is common in enterprise integration and task systems (Celery commonly sits on it).

Everyday analogy. SQS is a post office box you do not maintain; RabbitMQ is a sorting room with labelled slots you configure.

Common interview traps.

  • Visibility timeout shorter than processing time, causing duplicates.
  • Assuming SQS Standard keeps order.
  • Forgetting a DLQ, so a poison message loops forever.

notes.title: Kafka basics: topics, partitions, consumer groups
notes.html:
A Kafka topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log. A consumer group shares a topic: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group.

  • Parallelism = number of partitions. 12 partitions means at most 12 active consumers per group. A 13th sits idle.
  • Different groups are independent and each gets every message (this is how pub/sub works on Kafka).
  • When consumers join or leave, a rebalance reassigns partitions; processing pauses for a moment (cooperative rebalancing in newer clients reduces this).

Worked example. A topic of 6 partitions with 3 consumers: each gets 2 partitions. Add 3 more consumers: each gets 1. Add a 7th: it stays idle. If you need more throughput than 6 consumers give, you must add partitions (which changes key-to-partition mapping for new messages).

Industry examples. LinkedIn (origin), Uber (trip events, dispatch), Netflix (data pipeline, Keystone), Swiggy and Flipkart event buses.

Everyday analogy. A multi-lane road where each lane has one toll booth (consumer in the group); another company's convoy (another group) can drive the whole road independently.

Common interview traps.

  • More consumers than partitions does not speed things up.
  • Believing the broker tracks which consumer processed what; the group stores offsets per partition.

notes.title: Ordering guarantees
notes.html:
Kafka orders messages only within a single partition. Across partitions there is no global order. To keep the order for one entity (an order ID, a user), use that entity as the message key: partition = hash(key) mod numPartitions, so all its events land on the same partition.

  • Producer config for ordering with retries: enable.idempotence=true (also max.in.flight.requests.per.connection<=5) so a retry cannot reorder or duplicate.
  • Consumers must process a partition sequentially. Handing messages to a thread pool destroys order unless you shard by key.
  • SQS FIFO orders per MessageGroupId. RabbitMQ orders per queue per single consumer; multiple consumers or requeues break it.

Decision gravity. Choosing the key is nearly a one-way door: changing partition count remaps keys, and per-key order can be violated during the change. Pick a key with high cardinality and even spread; country as a key makes hot partitions.

Worked example. Events for order 42: created, paid, shipped. Key = order ID keeps them in order. With random keys, shipped can be processed before paid by another consumer.

Industry examples. Banks key by account ID; Uber keys trip events by trip ID.

Everyday analogy. All pages of one document go through one scanner in order; different documents can use different scanners.

Common interview traps.

  • Promising total ordering across a topic.
  • Increasing partitions "to scale" without thinking about key remapping.
  • Retries without idempotence causing reordering.

notes.title: When to use which
notes.html:
Pick by the job, not by the brand.

Need Pick Why
Simple background jobs on AWS, no ops SQS (+DLQ) Managed, scales, cheap
Complex routing, priorities, per-message TTL RabbitMQ Exchanges and bindings
Many consumers need same events, replay, high throughput Kafka Log, retention, partitions
Streaming analytics, event sourcing Kafka / Kinesis Ordered log
Very low volume, simple DB table or Redis list Do not over-build

Worked example. E-commerce: "send receipt email" (one consumer, retry, DLQ) fits SQS. "Order placed" event that billing, inventory, search, analytics and fraud all read, and which you may replay after a fraud-model bug, fits Kafka.

Operational cost. Kafka needs expertise (brokers, partitions, ISR tuning) or a managed service (MSK, Confluent Cloud); SQS is nearly zero ops. Cost of mistake: moving later is a migration project.

Industry examples. Many companies run both: Kafka as the event backbone, SQS/Rabbit for task queues.

Everyday analogy. A pickup truck for errands (SQS) versus a freight train system with timetables (Kafka).

Common interview traps.

  • Defaulting to Kafka for 10 messages per second.
  • Using a queue as a database or for data you must query.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Queues decouple time, speed and scale; always size backlog growth and drain time.
  • Queue deletes on consume; log retains and lets many groups replay by offset.
  • SQS: visibility timeout, DLQ, Standard (unordered, at-least-once) vs FIFO (ordered per group). RabbitMQ: exchanges, bindings, acks.
  • Kafka: partitions give parallelism and per-partition order; one consumer per partition per group.
  • Order requires a key; partition count changes remap keys.
  • Choose by workload: tasks to SQS/Rabbit, shared replayable events to Kafka.

questions.promptHtml: What is the core difference between a message queue like SQS or RabbitMQ and a log like Kafka?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Calling Kafka "a faster queue" is the classic miss; the answer drives replay, fan-out and design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A queue deletes a message once it is acknowledged, and each message goes to one consumer: it distributes jobs. A log is an append-only ordered file kept for a retention period; consumers only track an offset, so many independent readers can read the same data and replay by resetting the offset. Queue for "do this job once", log for "many systems need these events, and I may replay".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Queue:  Producer -> [m3 m2 m1] -> Consumer (ack => m1 gone)
Log:    Producer -> [m1 m2 m3 m4 ...]  Reader A @offset 2, Reader B @offset 4

In a log, a slow consumer deletes nothing; it just lags, and lag is a metric. Retention (time or size) is the storage cost. Replay after a bug is an offset reset. In a queue, replay means re-publishing and each extra consumer system needs its own queue (fan-out via exchange or SNS-to-SQS). Moving later from queue to log changes ack semantics, ordering and consumer code: close to a one-way door.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Kafka is just a faster queue".
  • Using a queue where several teams need the same events.
  • Forgetting that log retention is also a cost and a compliance question (PII).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you do pub/sub on a queue? -> Fan-out: RabbitMQ fanout exchange or SNS to several SQS queues.
  2. How do you do competing consumers on Kafka? -> A consumer group splits partitions among members.
  3. What does "lag" mean? -> Latest offset minus the group's committed offset, per partition.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names the products. Senior: explains retention, offsets, replay, fan-out and migration cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team built search indexing and analytics on SQS copies; adding a third consumer meant a new queue, and a bug fix needed re-publishing a week of events they had deleted.

questions.promptHtml: How do partitions and consumer groups work in Kafka, and what limits consumer parallelism?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core Kafka scaling model; wrong answers lead to "just add consumers".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A topic is split into partitions, each an ordered log. In a consumer group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer, so parallelism is at most the number of partitions: 12 partitions allow 12 active consumers; a 13th sits idle. Different groups are independent and each receives every message. When members join or leave, a rebalance reassigns partitions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
topic orders: P0 P1 P2 P3 P4 P5
group A (3 consumers): c1 {P0,P1}  c2 {P2,P3}  c3 {P4,P5}
group B (1 consumer):  b1 {P0..P5}   (independent copy of the stream)

Offsets are committed per group per partition (stored in the internal __consumer_offsets topic). Rebalance pauses processing; cooperative sticky assignment reduces the pause. If you need more parallelism than partitions, you must add partitions, which changes the key-to-partition mapping for new messages.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
props.put("group.id", "billing");
props.put("enable.auto.commit", "false");
consumer.subscribe(List.of("orders"));
while (true) {
    for (var r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) handle(r);
    consumer.commitSync();           // after the work, not before
}
props["group.id"] = "billing"
props["enable.auto.commit"] = "false"
consumer.subscribe(listOf("orders"))
while (true) {
    consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).forEach { handle(it) }
    consumer.commitSync()            // after the work, not before
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• More consumers than partitions to "scale".
  • Committing offsets before processing (loses messages on a crash).
  • Believing the broker tracks which consumer processed what; it tracks group offsets only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What triggers a rebalance? -> Member join/leave/crash, missed max.poll.interval.ms, partition count change.
  2. How do you scale a consumer that is CPU bound with 6 partitions? -> More partitions, or fan out within a consumer by key to threads while preserving per-key order.
  3. At-least-once vs at-most-once here? -> Commit after processing gives at-least-once; before gives at-most-once.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "consumers share the topic". Senior: partition ceiling, commit placement, rebalance cost and independence of groups.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team ran 40 consumers on a 12-partition topic and wondered why lag did not improve.

questions.contextHtml: A flash sale produces 5,000 orders/s for 90 seconds, then drops to 300/s. The email/receipt worker pool can process 800 messages/s (each 1 KB). Normal traffic is 300/s. The product owner wants the receipt email within 10 minutes of the order for 99% of orders. Queue is SQS Standard.
questions.promptHtml: Will a queue meet the 10-minute target? How big does the backlog get and when does it drain? What would you change if not?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A queue handles bursts, it will be fine." No numbers on growth and drain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 800/s limit CPU, the email provider rate limit or the DB? Can workers autoscale and how fast? Are receipts prioritized (payment confirmations first)? What is the message retention?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (capacity planning); I would set an alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Backlog grows during the sale and drains slowly because the spare capacity (800 minus 300) is small.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test the worker for sustained throughput; check the email provider limits.
  5. Root cause / math: During the burst the backlog grows by (5,000 - 800) = 4,200/s over 90 s = 378,000 messages (about 378 MB at 1 KB). After the burst, arrivals are 300/s and workers drain at 800 - 300 = 500/s net, so drain time = 378,000 / 500 = 756 s, about 12.6 min. The last order of the burst waits about 12.6 min: it misses the 10-minute target. Oldest message in the queue at the end of the burst waited 378,000/800 = 472 s, so the worst case is about 8 min for the first messages, and the 99th percentile lands around 12 min.
  6. Fix: Double workers to 1,600/s: net drain 1,300/s, drain 291 s, worst wait about 4.9 min. Autoscale on queue depth. Check the email provider limit does not cap it. Prioritise payment receipts on a separate queue.
  7. Prevention: Alarm on oldest-message age (above 5 min) and depth; load-test with the sale profile.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not size for the average rate. More workers cost money for a few minutes; autoscaling trades cost for lag. The user still gets an instant "order placed".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Workers autoscale takes 3 min to start? -> Pre-scale before the sale or keep a floor; recompute with the delay.
  • The email provider caps at 600/s? -> The cap is the real limit; add a second provider or batching.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sale's backlog took 40 minutes to drain because nobody divided backlog by net drain rate; receipts arrived after customers had already complained.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "queues absorb bursts".
  • Hire: computes backlog and drain time and finds the SLO miss.
  • Strong hire: handles provider limits, autoscale lag, prioritization and the oldest-age alarm.

questions.contextHtml: A video-transcoding service on SQS Standard sees customers getting two copies of the same output and the bill for compute doubling. A transcode takes 30 s to 4 min. Queue settings: visibility timeout 30 s (default), no DLQ. CloudWatch: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible oscillates; NumberOfMessagesReceived is 1.8x NumberOfMessagesDeleted. Red herring: the producer sometimes retries on 5xx.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "SQS delivers duplicates, nothing to do." It misses the visibility timeout interplay with job time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the p99 job duration? Does the worker delete the message only after finishing? Is the output idempotent (same key)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the visibility timeout to 300 s (above the max job time) via set-queue-attributes; stop the extra compute.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) timeout 30 s is shorter than jobs; messages reappear while worker 1 is busy; (b) producer retry duplicates; (c) worker crash mid-job.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare receives vs deletes (1.8x is the sign); log ApproximateReceiveCount per job; dedupe by job ID on the producer side.
  5. Root cause: After 30 s the message becomes visible again; worker 2 receives it and starts the same job; both finish, both write output.
  6. Fix: Timeout above max duration, or extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility heartbeats every 20 s; make the job idempotent: output key jobId, with a conditional write (if not exists) and a status table; add a DLQ with maxReceiveCount 5.
  7. Prevention: Alarm on receives/deletes ratio and DLQ depth; load test with the slowest job.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A very long timeout (hours) delays redelivery after a real crash, so heartbeat extension is better. FIFO queues would give dedup within 5 minutes but do not fix long jobs; idempotency is the real answer since delivery is at-least-once.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A job takes 40 min sometimes? -> Heartbeat extension with a cap (max 12 hours) or switch to a workflow engine.
  • Poison message crashes workers? -> The DLQ catches it after 5 receives.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A doubled compute bill was explained by a timeout default nobody changed; the heartbeat fix paid for itself in a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts duplicates.
  • Hire: fixes timeout and adds DLQ.
  • Strong hire: idempotent outputs, heartbeats and ratio-based alarms.

questions.contextHtml: An e-commerce company wants two features: (1) "send receipt email" after an order, one consumer, retries and failure handling; (2) an "OrderPlaced" event that billing, inventory, search indexing, analytics and a fraud model all consume, where the fraud model is retrained monthly and must replay the last 30 days. Volume: 800 orders/s at peak. The team has no Kafka experience and runs on AWS. An architect proposes "one Kafka for everything".
questions.promptHtml: What do you pick for each and what is the decision gravity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Kafka for everything because it scales." It ignores operations cost and that task queues do not need a log.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Event size and retention need? Ordering needs per order? Do consumers need to be added often? Is a managed service allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Receipt: task distribution (SQS + DLQ). Events: many readers plus replay (log).
  4. How I'd verify each: Estimate volume: 800/s x 1 KB x 86,400 x 30 days = about 2 TB (compressible, replicated x3 = larger): fine for a managed Kafka (MSK/Confluent). Receipt at 800/s is trivial for SQS.
  5. Root cause / reasoning: A queue deletes after consume; five consumers plus replay need a log. A task with retries needs ack/DLQ semantics, not a log.
  6. Fix / recommendation: SQS for receipts; managed Kafka (or Kinesis) for OrderPlaced, keyed by orderId; a consumer group per downstream system; the fraud team replays by resetting offsets or reads from a data-lake copy if the 30-day retention is costly.
  7. Prevention: A single event contract (schema registry) and DLQs per consumer.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Kafka as the only system makes simple jobs heavy; two systems means two skill sets. Gravity: the event backbone is close to one-way (consumer semantics, partition keys); the task queue is easy to swap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Team refuses to operate Kafka? -> Managed service, or SNS fan-out to SQS queues and accept no native replay (archive events to S3 for replay).
  • Volume 100/s only? -> SNS+SQS may be enough; do not over-build.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company moved all queues to Kafka for consistency and spent a quarter rebuilding retry/DLQ handling it had in SQS for free.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one tool, no reasoning.
  • Hire: SQS for tasks, Kafka for shared replayable events.
  • Strong hire: volume math, managed options, gravity, replay alternatives.

questions.contextHtml:
Consumer group payments-indexer on topic payments (12 partitions) has growing lag: 4.2M messages and rising 5,000/s. The team scaled the deployment from 8 to 20 pods; lag did not change. kafka-consumer-groups --describe:

GROUP             TOPIC     PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG      CONSUMER-ID
payments-indexer  payments  0          9812000         9990000         178000   c-1
payments-indexer  payments  1          9500100         9980000         479900   c-2
...
payments-indexer  payments  11         9700500         9970000         269500   c-12

Pods 13 to 20 show 0 assigned partitions. Each message takes 4 ms to index.
questions.promptHtml: Why did scaling fail and what is the right fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more pods" or "increase fetch size" without the partition arithmetic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the produce rate? Does indexing need per-key order? Can partitions be added (key remap implications)? Is the work CPU or I/O?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise per-consumer throughput: batch writes to the index (bulk API) and process messages of one partition in parallel by key within the consumer.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Partition ceiling (12 consumers max); slow per-message I/O (4 ms x 250 msg/s = 100% of a thread); rebalance churn.
  4. How I'd verify each: The describe output shows 8 idle pods; check per-partition throughput: 1/0.004 = 250 msg/s per consumer x 12 = 3,000 msg/s; produce rate = 3,000 + 5,000 = 8,000/s.
  5. Root cause: Parallelism is capped by 12 partitions; the arrival rate is 8,000/s vs a capacity of 3,000/s.
  6. Fix: Short term: bulk indexing (e.g. 500 documents per call; verify the real per-call latency, since the target is 8,000/s over 12 consumers, about 670/s each); or multi-thread per partition keyed by ID to keep per-key order. Long term: create a new topic with 48 partitions and migrate (so key mapping changes are planned) or add partitions with a replay plan.
  7. Prevention: Provision partitions for the target peak consumers (rule: peak throughput / per-consumer throughput x headroom 2); alert on lag growth rate, not just absolute lag.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just add partitions on the live topic: keys remap and per-key order breaks briefly. I would not drop max.poll.records blindly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is lag uneven per partition? -> Skewed keys or one slow consumer.
  • Adding partitions kills ordering? -> For new messages the key maps to a different partition than old ones; drain old first or use a new topic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team doubled pods three times before reading the describe output; the fix was a bulk index call, which gave 10x per consumer.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more pods.
  • Hire: spots the 12-partition ceiling and does the arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: batching, keyed parallelism, partition planning and migration plan.

questions.promptHtml: What ordering does Kafka guarantee, and how do you get per-entity order with retries and multiple consumers?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Kafka preserves order" is a half-truth; the details decide correctness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Only within one partition. For per-entity order I use the entity ID as the message key so all its events hash to the same partition: partition = hash(key) mod numPartitions. On the producer I set enable.idempotence=true so retries cannot duplicate or reorder (with max in-flight at most 5). The consumer must process a partition sequentially; handing messages to a random thread pool breaks order.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
key=order42: created -> paid -> shipped  => all in partition 3, read in order
key=null:    spread round-robin           => no per-order order

Changing the partition count changes hash(key) mod N, so new events for a key may land on a different partition than its old ones, and order can break during the transition. Key choice is a near one-way door: high cardinality, even spread. country as a key creates hot partitions. SQS FIFO orders per MessageGroupId; RabbitMQ orders per queue per single consumer (requeue and multiple consumers break it).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
acks=all
enable.idempotence=true
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Promising total order across a topic.
  • Adding partitions to "scale" without thinking about key remapping.
  • A thread pool in the consumer that reorders events of the same key.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get a global order? -> One partition (a throughput ceiling) or a sequence number and re-sequencing downstream.
  2. What does idempotence give? -> Per-partition exactly-once append from one producer session; not end-to-end exactly-once.
  3. What if a consumer fails mid-batch? -> It re-reads from the last committed offset: duplicates are possible; handle idempotently.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "partition key keeps order". Senior: adds idempotence, sequential per-partition processing, key cardinality and the repartition hazard.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shipped event got processed before paid because a consumer fanned messages to 16 threads with no key sharding.

questions.promptHtml: Queues are "at-least-once". What does that mean for consumer design, and how do DLQs and idempotency fit in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real systems fail partway; this tests the habit of designing for duplicates and poison messages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: At-least-once means a message is delivered one or more times: if I do not ack in time (visibility timeout in SQS, no ack in RabbitMQ), it is redelivered. So handlers must be idempotent, for example by recording a processed ID or making the write conditional. Messages that fail repeatedly go to a dead-letter queue after maxReceiveCount so one poison message does not block or loop forever.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SQS Standard: at-least-once, best-effort order. FIFO: strict order per MessageGroupId and dedup within a 5-minute window through MessageDeduplicationId, with lower throughput (verify current quotas). RabbitMQ: manual acks, unacked messages are redelivered, quorum queues replicate.

{ "RedrivePolicy": { "deadLetterTargetArn": "arn:aws:sqs:...:orders-dlq", "maxReceiveCount": 5 },
  "VisibilityTimeout": 60 }

Idempotency patterns: unique constraint on (messageId), INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, conditional update with a version, natural idempotent operations (set, not increment). Exactly-once effects = at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Visibility timeout shorter than processing time.
  • No DLQ, or a DLQ nobody monitors.
  • Idempotency key stored after the side effect, leaving a crash window.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you store the dedup record? -> Same DB transaction as the effect, so both commit or neither does.
  2. DLQ messages pile up: now what? -> Alert, inspect, fix, then redrive.
  3. Does SQS FIFO give exactly-once? -> Within the dedup window at the queue; consumer side still needs idempotency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use a DLQ". Senior: transactional dedup, redrive process, alarms and the failure window.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payment consumer without idempotency charged some customers twice after a timeout-driven redelivery.

questions.contextHtml:
Customers occasionally see an order as "Shipped" and then "Paid" in their timeline. Events are keyed by orderId on a 24-partition Kafka topic (producer config acks=1, retries=5, max.in.flight=5, idempotence off). The consumer:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
while (true) {
    for (var r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200))) {
        pool.submit(() -> timeline.apply(r.value()));   // parallel handling
    }
    consumer.commitSync();                              // commits before tasks finish
}
val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16)
while (true) {
    consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).forEach { r ->
        pool.submit { timeline.apply(r.value()) }       // parallel handling
    }
    consumer.commitSync()                               // commits before tasks finish
}
questions.promptHtml: List every way order and delivery can break here, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase partitions" or "add sleep". It misses the thread pool and the commit-before-work bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the timeline need strict order or is a per-event timestamp enough? Is handling idempotent? How many events per order per second?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Sort the timeline by event time on read; reduce the pool to 1 per partition.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the pool reorders events of the same key; (b) offsets committed before the work finishes (crash loses events); (c) producer retries with idempotence off and in-flight 5 can reorder a batch on the broker; (d) acks=1 loses events on leader failover.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log partition, offset and thread per event for one order; replay a crash test; check producer metrics for retries.
  5. Root cause: Events of one order are in order in the partition, but two consumer threads apply paid and shipped concurrently; either may finish first. The commit after poll also marks them done before they are.
  6. Fix: Consumer: process each partition sequentially, or shard to worker threads by hash(key) % N so one key always uses one thread, and commit only offsets whose work completed (per-partition watermark). Producer: enable.idempotence=true, acks=all. Add a version or sequence number to the event and ignore older versions in timeline.apply.
  7. Prevention: A test that publishes shuffled concurrent events for one key; a lint rule: no executor submit inside a poll loop without key-sharding.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set the pool to 1 for the whole group: key-sharded workers keep throughput. Sequence numbers cost a field but make the system robust to every remaining edge case.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A thread crashes after commit? -> Event lost; hence commit after completion with a watermark.
  • Rebalance during processing? -> Use a rebalance listener to finish or abandon in-flight work and commit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A subtle "paid after shipped" bug was a thread pool added for speed; per-key sharding kept the speedup and the order.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks partitions.
  • Hire: finds the pool and commit bugs and the fix by key sharding.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotence, acks=all, event versioning and rebalance handling.

questions.subtopic: hot partition from a bad key
questions.contextHtml: A ride-hailing platform keys driver-location events by city. The topic has 60 partitions, 50,000 events/s total. Mumbai makes up 30% of events (15,000/s), Delhi 20%. Consumers handle 2,500 events/s each. Lag is zero for most partitions but 3 partitions show growing lag; one consumer is at 100% CPU, with the topic's max lag at 2.4M. Next quarter volume is 10x for a festival. Red herring: broker disk usage is balanced.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the lag pattern and redesign the key and capacity.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add partitions or consumers." Cities still hash to one partition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What order do consumers need: per driver, per city or none? Do consumers aggregate by city? What is the freshness need (location is useless after 10 s)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop or sample stale events on the hot partitions (consumers skip events older than 10 s); temporarily raise the throughput on the hot consumer via batching.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hot key (city) pinning 15,000 events/s to one partition; poor hashing (unlikely); slow consumer (the CPU shows it is busy, but only because it is flooded).
  4. How I'd verify each: Bytes-in per partition (kafka-log-dirs or broker metrics); count of events per key; lag by partition.
  5. Root cause: hash("Mumbai") mod 60 is one partition: 15,000 events/s against a 2,500/s consumer. Partition count is irrelevant for one key. At 10x it would be 150,000/s into one partition.
  6. Fix: Key by driverId (high cardinality, ordering needed per driver only). Where a city aggregation is needed, a second stage re-keys by city using a stream processor with a pre-aggregation, or key by city#bucket (random 0-N) and merge downstream. Partitions: 50k x 10 = 500k/s / 2,500 = 200 consumers: plan 256 partitions on a new topic with a migration.
  7. Prevention: Key-cardinality review in design docs; a dashboard of partition skew (max/mean) with an alert above 2x.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: City-level order across drivers is not needed and is not worth a hot partition. Re-keying changes the order scope; adding partitions to the old topic would remap keys without helping the hot one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Consumers need all events of a city together? -> Fan-in stage with pre-aggregation by city#bucket.
  • 256 partitions overhead? -> More file handles and a longer rebalance; keep it moderate, verify broker limits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "keyed by tenant" topic had one tenant at 60% of traffic; the key became tenant#hash(userId) mod 16, and the lag disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: add consumers or partitions.
  • Hire: identifies the hot key and changes the key to a high-cardinality one.
  • Strong hire: capacity at 10x, aggregation stage, stale-event dropping and skew alerts.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident: at 03:10 a malformed message (amount: null) entered an SQS queue feeding the billing worker. The worker threw an exception before deleting it. Visibility timeout was 30 s, no DLQ. The message was received 11,000 times over 91 hours; each attempt wrote a partial row and sent an alert email. Worse, the exception path also released a DB lock late and the queue depth tripled as 40 workers kept failing. Metrics: error rate 100% for that message, 3% overall; DB lock waits up 6x.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, timeline lessons, and the specific changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A bad message; validate input next time." It stops at one fix and has no systemic changes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who produced the message and what validation exists? Why did nobody see 91 hours? Is the handler idempotent (partial row)? Are alerts rate-limited?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the message to a DLQ manually (or delete it after copying it to a bucket); clean partial rows; throttle alert emails.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: No DLQ; no validation at producer or consumer boundary; non-transactional handler leaves partial writes; alert has no dedupe.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check queue attributes (RedrivePolicy missing); ApproximateReceiveCount on the message; handler code path for the transaction.
  5. Root cause: Poison message plus at-least-once redelivery plus no DLQ gave an infinite loop. Contributing: no schema validation, partial writes, noisy alert instead of a metric on receive count, and low visibility of oldest-message age.
  6. Fix: DLQ with maxReceiveCount 5 and an alarm on DLQ depth > 0; schema validation at the producer plus the consumer (reject to DLQ immediately for permanent errors, retry with backoff for transient ones); wrap handler work in one DB transaction with an idempotency key; exponential backoff by changing visibility on failure.
  7. Prevention: Runbook for redrive; dashboards: receive-count p99, oldest age; contract tests on message schemas; a chaos test that injects a malformed message.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not lower the receive count to 1 (transient errors would drop good messages), and not add a blanket try/catch that swallows errors and deletes data silently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The DLQ message must still be processed after a fix? -> Redrive it after the handler is fixed (SQS redrive to source).
  • Retry storm when the DB is down? -> Circuit breaker and backoff so workers stop pulling instead of failing 40-wide.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The cheapest lasting fix in such an incident was an alarm: "DLQ depth > 0 or any message received more than 5 times".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "validate input".
  • Hire: DLQ, validation, transaction, alarms.
  • Strong hire: separates permanent from transient errors, backoff and breakers, runbook and chaos test.

questions.contextHtml: A logistics company runs RabbitMQ (topic exchange, 6 queues, 25,000 msg/s peak, quorum queues) for shipment events. Three new teams (ETA model, billing audit, customer notifications) want the same events, one needs a 14-day replay. The broker is at 70% CPU and adding queues for each consumer duplicated the publish work. Existing consumers rely on per-shipment order and use priorities on one queue. Zero downtime is required; the producers are 11 services.
questions.promptHtml: Should you move to Kafka, and how would you migrate safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, Kafka is better; cut over on a weekend." No replay of semantics, no phased plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do consumers need priorities or per-message TTL (Kafka lacks them)? Are routing needs complex? Who owns each consumer? What is the max acceptable duplicate window? Team skill and managed options?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce broker load now: for the new consumers use a fanout bridge, not 3 extra queues copying work.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The need is fan-out plus replay (log fits); priority and routing features of RabbitMQ are used by one queue (keep it there); order per shipment maps to key = shipmentId.
  4. How I'd verify each: Inventory the consumers' semantics; measure the event size and 14-day volume: 25k/s x 1 KB x 14 d = about 30 TB at peak rate (real average is lower; verify) so check storage cost and tiered storage.
  5. Root cause / reasoning: Queue-based fan-out multiplies work for each reader and offers no replay. A log decouples reader count from broker work.
  6. Fix / plan: (1) Stand up a managed Kafka; topic shipments keyed by shipmentId, partitions sized for peak consumers. (2) Bridge: a Rabbit consumer republishes events to Kafka, new consumers read Kafka only. (3) Producers dual-publish one service at a time behind a flag with an event ID for dedup. (4) Migrate old consumers one at a time to Kafka with idempotent handlers; run in parallel and compare outputs. (5) Retire the bridge; keep Rabbit for priority/TTL queue tasks.
  7. Prevention: A schema registry and event versioning; per-consumer lag SLOs; rollback per consumer.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do a big-bang cutover or force priorities onto Kafka. Cost: ops complexity and storage; gravity: consumers' semantics change from ack-and-delete to offsets, so this is close to a one-way door per consumer, which is why the migration is incremental.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Duplicates during dual publish? -> Consumers dedupe by event ID; the bridge preserves IDs.
  • Per-shipment order across the bridge? -> The bridge must publish keyed by shipmentId and process sequentially per queue.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The migration that worked ran a bridge for two months; the one that failed removed it after a week and found a consumer nobody had inventoried.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang cutover.
  • Hire: bridge, phased migration, keyed order.
  • Strong hire: also questions whether to move everything, quantifies storage, dedupe by event ID, consumer inventory and rollback.
